error_modes.label: Takeoff airspeed at rotation and lift-off

texts.0: SP, due to an aft stick input applied without reference to the airspeed indication, did not execute the takeoff with the standard airspeed. The aircraft was rotated below the computed rotation speed, against a criterion that allows no tolerance on the low side, and the airspeed then overshot the standard by more than 10 knots in the initial climb. IP intervened on the controls to set the takeoff attitude and to recover the airspeed to the standard value.
texts.1: SP, due to a late transition of the scan from the runway to the airspeed indication during the ground roll, did not execute the takeoff with the standard airspeed. The airspeed settled about 10 knots above standard, at the outer limit of the allowed one-sided tolerance, and SP reduced the excess only after two verbal prompts from IP. The delayed correction carried the fast condition through the initial climb.
texts.2: SP, due to a rotation input applied slightly later than the computed speed required, allowed the takeoff airspeed to build past the standard. The excess reached roughly 7 knots, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, and SP identified the deviation on the indicator and reset the takeoff attitude on personal initiative. No prompting and no IP control input were required.
texts.3: SP executed the takeoff with the standard airspeed, rotating on the computed speed with no deviation on the low side and holding the excess inside 5 knots. The scan alternated continuously between the runway and the airspeed indication, and the pitch corrections were small and immediate.
texts.4: SP rotated precisely at the computed takeoff speed and held the standard airspeed through the transition, with deviations that were negligible against the published tolerance. Control inputs were smooth and progressive, and the airspeed never trended toward the low side where no tolerance exists.
texts.marginal: SP kept the takeoff airspeed inside standards but consistently on the fast side, with the excess sitting in the upper part of the acceptable band on every takeoff of the sortie. The trend came from anticipating the rotation callout late rather than from control technique, and it repeated without further degradation. SP is expected to start the rotation input on the computed speed so that the takeoff airspeed is centered on standard.

texts_at.0: SP rotated and accelerated through the takeoff roll with the IP calling the rotation speed and confirming the airspeed trend on the indicator, due to first exposure to holding a scan between the runway and the airspeed indication through rotation. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to rotate at the computed speed and hold the takeoff airspeed independently on the next sortie, without the rotation speed or the trend being called out.
texts_at.1: SP rotated at the computed speed and held the takeoff airspeed to the level expected at this stage, with the excess settling about 10 knots fast, near the upper part of the one-sided tolerance, due to the scan transitioning from the runway to the airspeed indication a beat later than the rotation call. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to move the scan to the airspeed indication earlier in the ground roll so the excess sits with more margin below the tolerance.
texts_at.2: SP reset the takeoff attitude and held the airspeed excess to about 7 knots fast, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, due to a rotation input applied a fraction later than the computed speed required. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to begin the rotation input exactly on the computed speed rather than a fraction after it.
texts_at.3: SP rotated on the computed speed and held the takeoff airspeed excess to about 5 knots fast, due to the pitch correction through the transition being a shade later than the ideal timing though still well inside the tighter tolerance. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to make the pitch correction at the same instant the rotation input is applied.

texts_above.1: SP rotated on the computed speed and brought the takeoff airspeed excess down to about 9 knots fast, near the upper part of the one-sided tolerance, before the initial climb was established. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP identified an airspeed excess building past standard on the takeoff roll and reset the takeoff attitude, containing it to about 7 knots fast on personal initiative and with no prompting. Moving the scan to the airspeed indication earlier in the ground roll, before the excess builds at all, would remove the correction from the sequence entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good airspeed control at rotation.
texts_above.3: SP rotated on the computed speed with no deviation on the low side and held the airspeed excess to about 3 knots fast, with the scan alternating continuously between the runway and the airspeed indication. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good rotation technique.
texts_above.4: SP rotated precisely on the computed speed and held the takeoff airspeed excess to a knot or two, with control inputs smooth and progressive throughout the transition. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent airspeed control at rotation.

error_modes.label: Runway centerline tracking during the takeoff roll
error_modes.source: specific:Maintain in the center line of RWY (ft)

texts.0: SP, due to rudder input insufficient for the yaw produced at power application and for the reported crosswind, did not maintain the A/C at the centerline during T/O. Lateral displacement passed 10 feet and continued to diverge toward the runway edge as the aircraft accelerated. IP took the controls to re-establish the takeoff track before rotation.
texts.1: SP, due to rudder corrections applied in discrete steps instead of continuously, did not maintain the A/C at the centerline during T/O. Displacement reached about 10 feet, at the limit of the allowed deviation, and SP re-centered the aircraft only after IP called for rudder. The aircraft lifted off with the track still offset from the centerline.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow initial response to the swing at power application, drifted off the runway centerline by roughly 8 feet. The deviation remained between the code 3 and code 1 limits and SP corrected it with coordinated rudder well before rotation, with no prompting and no IP action.
texts.3: SP maintained the A/C at the centerline during T/O with lateral deviation held inside 5 feet. Rudder inputs were continuous and matched to the yaw produced by power application and wind, and the same track was carried through rotation and lift-off.
texts.4: SP held the aircraft on the runway centerline with deviations that were barely perceptible against the runway markings. The directional control inputs anticipated the yaw rather than reacting to it, and the takeoff track was preserved unchanged into the initial climb.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft inside the centerline tolerance but with a persistent offset to one side that was held rather than removed for most of the ground roll. The offset stayed within standards and did not grow, but it left less margin than the technique should produce. SP is expected to re-center the aircraft as soon as the offset is detected instead of tracking parallel to the centerline.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the runway centerline during the takeoff roll with the IP calling the rudder correction needed against the swing at power application, due to first exposure to matching rudder pressure to the yaw produced as power comes up. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to track the centerline independently on the next takeoff roll, applying the rudder correction without it being called.
texts_at.1: SP held the takeoff roll to the level expected at this stage, correcting a centerline deviation of about 10 feet, at the upper part of the tolerance, due to rudder corrections applied in discrete steps rather than continuously against the yaw at power application. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply rudder as a continuous correction rather than in discrete steps.
texts_at.2: SP corrected a centerline deviation of roughly 7 feet with coordinated rudder well before rotation, due to a slightly slow initial response to the swing at power application. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the first rudder correction at the moment the swing begins rather than a beat after it.
texts_at.3: SP held lateral deviation to about 5 feet through the takeoff roll, due to the rudder input at power application being matched closely but not exactly to the yaw produced, well inside the tighter tolerance. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to match the rudder input to the yaw exactly rather than closely.

texts_above.1: SP corrected a centerline deviation and held the track to about 9 feet from the centerline, at the upper part of the allowed tolerance, through the remainder of the takeoff roll. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP for rudder. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP corrected a centerline drift of roughly 8 feet with coordinated rudder well before rotation, recognizing the slow initial response to the power-application swing on personal initiative. Anticipating the yaw at the moment power is applied, rather than responding to the drift once it appears, would remove the correction from the roll entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound directional control at takeoff.
texts_above.3: SP held lateral deviation inside 4 feet through the takeoff roll, with rudder inputs continuous and matched to the yaw produced by power application and wind, the same track carried through rotation and lift-off. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed directional control.
texts_above.4: SP held the aircraft on the runway centerline with deviations of a foot or two, barely perceptible against the runway markings, with directional inputs anticipating the yaw rather than reacting to it. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional directional control at takeoff.

error_modes.label: Line Up check and After Takeoff Checklist discipline

texts.0: SP, due to a lapse in which briefed items were omitted under workload, did not execute the LINE UP checks without omissions. Items bearing on the takeoff configuration were left unverified and the After Takeoff Checklist was not begun until the departure was well established. IP directed the completion of both checks and confirmed the configuration on behalf of SP.
texts.1: SP, due to a lapse under the workload accumulated at the hold-short line, did not execute the LINE UP checks without omissions. One item was left unchecked and was picked up only after IP prompted for it, and the After Takeoff Checklist was completed late, after the first turn of the departure. The omissions were recovered only through IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated the cockpit work into the last seconds before line up, initially skipped one item of the LINE UP checks. SP detected the omission on a self-initiated back-check and completed the item before brake release, without prompting. The After Takeoff Checklist was then run complete, slightly later than the optimum point but before the departure turn.
texts.3: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions and started the After Takeoff Checklist at the proper point of the departure. Each item was verified against the actual switch position or indication rather than recited from memory.
texts.4: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions and with a settled flow that left capacity for the takeoff clearance and the traffic picture. The After Takeoff Checklist was initiated at the correct point and completed without interrupting aircraft control or the departure profile.
texts.marginal: SP completed the LINE UP checks and the After Takeoff Checklist without omissions, but the checks were run so close to brake release that any interruption would have displaced an item. The standard was met on every takeoff of the sortie, with no item missed. SP is expected to complete the checks earlier in the sequence so that the flow retains margin for an interruption.

texts_at.0: SP worked through the LINE UP checks and the After Takeoff Checklist with the IP calling each remaining item in turn, due to first exposure to running both checks back to back under the workload of the hold-short line. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to run both checks independently at the next line up, completing every item without a call from the IP.
texts_at.1: SP executed the LINE UP checks and the After Takeoff Checklist to the level expected at this stage, with every item eventually verified, due to task sequencing that concentrated the cockpit work into the last seconds before line up and left the checklist running behind the departure turn. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to start the LINE UP checks earlier at the hold so the sequence is complete before brake release.
texts_at.2: SP completed the LINE UP checks without omission and ran the After Takeoff Checklist complete, due to one item of the LINE UP sequence being skipped on the first pass and caught on a self-initiated back-check before brake release. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to read each LINE UP item against the actual switch position on the first pass, without relying on a back-check to catch an omission.
texts_at.3: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions and started the After Takeoff Checklist at the proper point of the departure, due to the checklist being completed a few seconds later than the optimum point though still before the departure turn. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to move the After Takeoff Checklist to the optimum point identified in the technique.

texts_above.1: SP completed the LINE UP checks and the After Takeoff Checklist in full, with one item of the LINE UP sequence completed only once the gap was pointed out before brake release. The item was completed after a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP detected one skipped LINE UP item on a self-initiated back-check and completed it before brake release, then ran the After Takeoff Checklist complete, slightly later than the optimum point but before the departure turn. Verifying every item against the actual switch position on the first pass, rather than catching an omission on a back-check, would remove the need for that check. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid checklist discipline at line up.
texts_above.3: SP executed the LINE UP checks without omissions with a settled flow that left capacity for the takeoff clearance and the traffic picture, initiating the After Takeoff Checklist at the correct point without interrupting aircraft control. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed checklist management.
texts_above.4: SP ran the LINE UP checks and the After Takeoff Checklist without a single omission and with capacity left over for the takeoff clearance and the traffic picture, each check verified against the actual switch position rather than recited. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding checklist management.

error_modes.label: Engine run-up with the aircraft held stationary

texts.0: SP, due to brake pressure released before the power setting was verified, allowed movement of the A/C during the engine run-up. The aircraft crept forward while the engine indications were still being checked and displaced from the run-up position on the runway. IP intervened and directed an immediate power reduction to stop the movement.
texts.1: SP, due to brake pressure that decayed while attention was on the engine instruments, allowed a noticeable forward movement of the A/C during the engine run-up. SP restored brake pressure only after IP called the movement, and the takeoff roll was begun from a position displaced along the runway. The run-up check was completed under the correction rather than as briefed.
texts.2: SP, due to brake pressure applied unevenly on the two pedals, allowed a small forward movement to begin as run-up power was set. SP recognized it at once, restored full brake pressure and completed the engine indication check at the set power with no IP input. Brake release into the takeoff roll was then made from the correct position.
texts.3: SP allowed no movement of the A/C during the engine run-up, holding full brake pressure while the power was set. The engine indications were verified against the expected values and the brakes were released as a single positive action into the takeoff roll.
texts.4: SP allowed no movement of the A/C during the engine run-up, with full brake pressure held throughout and no attention diverted from the engine indications. Brake release was clean and the aircraft entered the takeoff roll straight from the exact run-up position.
texts.marginal: SP prevented any movement of the A/C during the engine run-up, but the brake pressure held was only just sufficient and the aircraft was on the point of creeping at the higher power settings. The criterion was met, with no displacement observed. SP is expected to set firm brake pressure before advancing the power so that the margin does not depend on the run-up being short.

texts_at.0: SP held the aircraft during the engine run-up with the IP calling for firm brake pressure as the power was advanced, due to first exposure to setting brake pressure ahead of a power increase rather than reacting to the aircraft once it moves. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to set firm brake pressure and hold the aircraft stationary independently at the next run-up, without a call for brake pressure.
texts_at.1: SP held the aircraft with only a small forward creep during the engine run-up, at the edge of what the criterion for no movement allows at this stage, due to brake pressure applied unevenly on the two pedals as the power was set. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply even brake pressure on both pedals before advancing power for the run-up.
texts_at.2: SP restored full brake pressure and completed the engine indication check with no further movement, due to brake pressure applied unevenly on the two pedals that let a small forward movement begin as run-up power was set. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to check that brake pressure is even on both pedals before the power is advanced, not after movement begins.
texts_at.3: SP allowed no movement of the aircraft during the engine run-up, due to brake pressure that was firm but reached its full value a moment after power began to come up rather than before it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set full brake pressure before the power lever starts moving, not while it is already advancing.

texts_above.1: SP held the aircraft through the engine run-up with only a brief forward creep as the power was set, the creep stopped once brake pressure was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a small forward movement beginning as run-up power was set, restored full brake pressure at once and completed the engine indication check with the aircraft stationary and no further input needed. Setting even pressure on both pedals before power is advanced, rather than after a small movement appears, would remove the correction from the run-up. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady brake control during run-up.
texts_above.3: SP allowed no movement of the aircraft during the engine run-up, holding full brake pressure while the power was set and verifying the engine indications against the expected values before releasing the brakes as a single positive action. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate run-up technique.
texts_above.4: SP held full brake pressure throughout the engine run-up with no attention diverted from the engine indications and no movement at any power setting, releasing the brakes cleanly into the takeoff roll from the exact run-up position. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary run-up discipline.

error_modes.label: Takeoff attitude and transition to climbing attitude

texts.0: SP, due to a rotation input applied at a rate the pitch reference could not be tracked at, did not bring and maintain the A/C to the proper T/O attitude. The aircraft was over-rotated past the takeoff attitude and the pitch then oscillated through the transition instead of settling at the proper climbing attitude. IP intervened on the controls to set the attitude and stop the oscillation.
texts.1: SP, due to pitch corrections made against the outside picture alone without reference to the attitude indication, did not maintain the proper T/O attitude. The aircraft was held at an attitude at the edge of the acceptable band and the resulting airspeed deviation reached the limit of tolerance, corrected only after repeated verbal direction from IP. The climbing attitude was established late in the departure.
texts.2: SP, due to a stick input that was released before the takeoff attitude was fully established, allowed the pitch to settle below the proper T/O attitude. The resulting airspeed deviation stayed between the code 3 and code 1 limits and SP reset the attitude and stabilized the climbing attitude independently, without prompting or IP control input.
texts.3: SP brought the A/C to the proper T/O attitude with a smooth rotation, maintained it through lift-off, and established the proper climbing attitude promptly. Pitch was held steady against both the outside picture and the attitude indication, keeping the airspeed inside the tighter tolerance.
texts.4: SP set the proper T/O attitude in one continuous input and held it with no perceptible pitch excursion through lift-off. The transition to the climbing attitude was made at the correct point and the attitude was then maintained with negligible deviation for the remainder of the departure.
texts.marginal: SP established and maintained the proper T/O and climbing attitudes within standards, but each attitude was reached through a small overshoot followed by a correction rather than being captured directly. The resulting airspeed excursions stayed inside tolerance and did not repeat in the same direction. SP is expected to capture the attitude on the first input, using the pitch reference rather than the airspeed trend to confirm it.

texts_at.0: SP brought the aircraft to the takeoff attitude and the climbing attitude with the IP calling the pitch reference and the point to begin each transition, due to first exposure to setting and holding an attitude by reference to the indication rather than the outside picture alone. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to set and hold both attitudes independently on the next departure, without the pitch reference being called.
texts_at.1: SP brought the aircraft to the takeoff attitude and then to the climbing attitude to the level expected at this stage, with the resulting airspeed held inside the wider tolerance, due to pitch corrections made mostly against the outside picture with only an occasional check of the attitude indication. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to cross-check the attitude indication on every correction rather than only occasionally.
texts_at.2: SP reset the takeoff attitude and stabilized the climbing attitude with the airspeed held inside the tighter tolerance, due to a stick input released a moment before the takeoff attitude was fully established, letting the pitch settle slightly low. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the stick input until the attitude is confirmed on the indicator, not release it early.
texts_at.3: SP established the takeoff attitude with a smooth rotation and the climbing attitude promptly after, due to the transition between the two attitudes being flown a beat slower than the ideal though still smooth and controlled. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to blend the transition into the rotation itself rather than pausing between the two attitudes.

texts_above.1: SP brought the aircraft to the takeoff attitude and then to the climbing attitude, with the resulting airspeed deviation held to the edge of the acceptable band before the attitude was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP reset the takeoff attitude after the pitch settled slightly low and stabilized the climbing attitude promptly, keeping the resulting airspeed deviation inside the tighter tolerance without prompting or any IP input. Holding the stick input until the attitude is confirmed on the indicator, rather than releasing it early, would remove the correction from the transition. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable attitude control on departure.
texts_above.3: SP set the proper takeoff attitude with a smooth rotation, maintained it through lift-off and established the climbing attitude promptly, holding pitch steady against both the outside picture and the attitude indication. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good attitude control.
texts_above.4: SP set the takeoff attitude in one continuous input with no perceptible pitch excursion through lift-off, transitioning to the climbing attitude at the correct point and holding it with negligible deviation for the rest of the departure. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior attitude control on departure.

error_modes.label: Gear and flap retraction within configuration speed limits

texts.0: SP, due to failure to monitor the aircraft state after the configuration change, did not clean the A/C configuration without violating the speed limit. The retraction was selected with the airspeed already beyond the placarded limit for the configuration and the deviation continued to increase while the indications went unchecked. IP intervened to reduce the pitch trend and to direct the correct sequence.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted cross-check of airspeed against the configuration in use, cleaned the A/C configuration right at the placarded speed limit. SP lowered the airspeed trend only after IP called the limit, and the retraction indications were confirmed late. The margin to the limit was recovered by prompting rather than by the SP's own scan.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check that returned to the airspeed later than the acceleration required, delayed the retraction until the airspeed had built close to the placarded limit. The margin was reduced but never violated, remaining between the code 3 and code 1 zones, and SP completed the cleanup and confirmed the indications without prompting or IP action.
texts.3: SP cleaned the A/C configuration at the correct points of the departure with the airspeed comfortably inside the placarded limits. Each selection was followed by a check of the corresponding indication before the scan moved on.
texts.4: SP retracted the landing gear and flaps at the briefed points with a wide margin to the placarded limits and confirmed both indications without interrupting the climb profile. The airspeed and configuration were cross-checked continuously so that no selection was made on assumption.
texts.marginal: SP cleaned the A/C configuration without violating any speed limit, but the selections were consistently made near the upper part of the available speed band. No limit was approached closely enough to constitute a deviation. SP is expected to make the retraction selections at the briefed points so that the margin to the placarded limits is set by the plan rather than by the correction.

texts_at.0: SP cleaned the aircraft configuration with the IP calling the airspeed against the placarded limit before each selection, due to first exposure to cross-checking airspeed continuously through an acceleration rather than at isolated points. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to cross-check the airspeed and clean the configuration independently on the next departure, without the limit being called before each selection.
texts_at.1: SP cleaned the aircraft configuration to the level expected at this stage, with the airspeed comfortably clear of the placarded limit by the time each selection was made, due to a cross-check of airspeed against configuration that was interrupted once during the acceleration. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to complete the airspeed cross-check without interruption through every configuration change.
texts_at.2: SP completed the cleanup and confirmed both retraction indications without prompting, due to a cross-check that returned to the airspeed later than the acceleration required, narrowing the margin to the placarded limit before the selections were made. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to return the cross-check to the airspeed indicator on the same rhythm as the acceleration, not after it has outpaced the scan.
texts_at.3: SP cleaned the aircraft configuration at the correct points of the departure with the airspeed comfortably inside the placarded limits, due to one indication being confirmed a beat after the corresponding selection rather than in the same glance. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm each indication in the same glance as the selection that produced it.

texts_above.1: SP cleaned the aircraft configuration with the margin to the placarded limit narrowed before the gear and flap selections were made, the margin recovered before either selection went out of limits. The recovery followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP completed the cleanup and confirmed both the gear and flap indications without prompting, recognizing that the cross-check had fallen behind the acceleration and narrowed the margin to the placarded limit before either selection was made. Returning the cross-check to the airspeed indicator on the same rhythm as the acceleration, rather than after it falls behind, would remove the narrowed margin altogether. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured configuration management.
texts_above.3: SP retracted the landing gear and flaps at the briefed points with a wide margin to the placarded limits, confirming both indications without interrupting the climb profile and cross-checking airspeed and configuration continuously. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise configuration management.
texts_above.4: SP retracted the landing gear and flaps at the briefed points with a wide margin to the placarded limits on every selection, cross-checking airspeed and configuration continuously so that no selection was ever made on assumption. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate configuration management.

error_modes.label: Acceleration to and maintenance of the standard climb airspeed

texts.0: SP, due to a pitch attitude held well above the value the climb profile required, did not accelerate and maintain the proper climb airspeed. The airspeed stopped short of the standard climb airspeed and then decayed further while the departure was continued. IP intervened on the controls to lower the pitch and re-establish the standard climb airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to pitch changes made in response to the airspeed trend rather than to a set attitude, did not maintain the proper climb airspeed. The airspeed oscillated out to the limit of the allowed deviation on each correction and was stabilized only after repeated verbal direction from IP. The standard climb airspeed was reached late in the departure segment.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly high pitch attitude held after the configuration was clean, allowed the climb airspeed to fall short of standard. The deviation remained between the code 3 and code 1 limits and SP recognized it, adjusted the attitude and re-established the standard climb airspeed on personal initiative, without IP input.
texts.3: SP accelerated the aircraft to the standard climb airspeed at the correct point and maintained it inside the tighter tolerance for the remainder of the departure. Pitch was set to a known attitude and trimmed, so the airspeed held without repeated correction.
texts.4: SP accelerated to the standard climb airspeed promptly after the aircraft was clean and held it with negligible deviation throughout the climb. The aircraft was trimmed accurately, and the airspeed required no correction once established.
texts.marginal: SP accelerated to and maintained the proper climb airspeed within standards, but the aircraft was flown slightly out of trim so that the airspeed required continuous small pitch corrections to stay there. The deviations never left the acceptable band. SP is expected to trim the aircraft once the climbing attitude is set, so that the standard climb airspeed is maintained without continuous input.

texts_at.0: SP accelerated to and held the climb airspeed with the IP calling the pitch attitude to set once the aircraft was clean, due to first exposure to trimming to a set attitude rather than adjusting pitch off the airspeed trend. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to set the climb attitude and hold the airspeed independently on the next departure, without the attitude being called.
texts_at.1: SP accelerated to and held the climb airspeed to the level expected at this stage, with the value reached slightly later in the departure than the optimum point, due to pitch changes made mostly in response to the airspeed trend rather than to a set attitude. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set a known climbing attitude first and let the airspeed settle from it, rather than chasing the airspeed with pitch.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the climb airspeed falling short of standard and re-established it on personal initiative, due to a slightly high pitch attitude held after the configuration was clean. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to check the pitch attitude against a known reference as soon as the configuration is clean, before the airspeed has a chance to fall short.
texts_at.3: SP accelerated the aircraft to the standard climb airspeed at the correct point and maintained it for the remainder of the departure, due to the trim being set a moment after the climbing attitude rather than at the same time. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to trim the aircraft in the same action as setting the climbing attitude.

texts_above.1: SP accelerated to the standard climb airspeed, with the value reached only after the airspeed had oscillated out to the edge of the allowed deviation on the first correction. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the climb airspeed falling short of standard after the configuration was cleaned and re-established it with a coordinated attitude adjustment, on personal initiative and with no input from IP. Checking the pitch attitude against a known reference the moment the configuration is clean, rather than after the airspeed has already fallen short, would remove the correction from the climb. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent climb-airspeed management.
texts_above.3: SP accelerated the aircraft to the standard climb airspeed at the correct point and held it inside the tighter tolerance for the remainder of the departure, with pitch set to a known attitude and trimmed so the airspeed held without repeated correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined climb-airspeed technique.
texts_above.4: SP accelerated to the standard climb airspeed promptly after the aircraft was clean and held it with negligible deviation throughout the climb, trimmed accurately enough that no further correction was required once established. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless climb-airspeed technique.

error_modes.label: Performance check against the calculated takeoff data

texts_at.3: SP verbalized the gear clear call before raising the gear and flaps and paused momentarily for the acknowledgement, due to the confirmation of the climb rate being made in the same breath as the call rather than clearly ahead of it, though still before the handle was moved. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the climb confirmation as a distinct step before the call rather than blending the two together.

texts_above.1: SP made the gear clear call and retracted the gear, with the climb rate and engine instruments confirmed only after being asked for rather than ahead of the call. The prompt came as a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized that the call had not left the momentary pause the technique requires, stopped, confirmed the climb by altimeter and VSI and the engine instruments within limits, and repeated the call properly before completing the cleanup, with no prompting or IP action needed. Completing the climb and engine-instrument confirmation fully before the call is made, rather than alongside it, would remove the need for that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent gear-clear sequencing.
texts_above.3: SP verbalized the gear clear call before raising the gear and flaps, paused momentarily for the acknowledgement and treated the retraction as a conscious, deliberate act, with the climb confirmed on the altimeter and VSI and the engine instruments checked within limits beforehand. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined gear-clear sequencing.
texts_above.4: SP made the gear clear call with the climb already confirmed on the altimeter and VSI, waited for the acknowledgement, then completed the retraction and the clean-configuration confirmation with no interruption to aircraft control and the departure profile unchanged. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless gear-clear sequencing.

error_modes.label: Minimum airspeed and altitude before the first turn after takeoff

texts.0: SP, due to starting the first turn after takeoff before passing the departure end of the runway, did not climb straight ahead as the technique requires. The turn was begun clearly below the minimum of 140 KIAS and below 700 feet AGL, so both gates were missed by a wide margin. IP intervened to roll the aircraft wings level and continue the climb until the minima were attained.
texts.1: SP, due to anticipating the departure instruction, began the first turn after takeoff with the airspeed and the altitude only just reaching 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL. The gates were met at the limit and the aircraft was rolled wings level again only after IP called for the climb to be continued straight ahead.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan concentrated on the turn point rather than on airspeed and altitude, started to bank before 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL had been confirmed. SP recognized the anticipation, rolled wings level and continued straight ahead until both values were attained, correcting without prompting and losing only a short segment of the departure track.
texts.3: SP climbed straight ahead until past the departure end of the runway and attained a minimum of 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL before the first turn after takeoff. Airspeed and altitude were confirmed before the bank was applied and the departure was flown as directed.
texts.4: SP flew the takeoff leg straight ahead past the departure end with 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL clearly attained and cross-checked before the first turn. The roll into the turn was smooth and coordinated and was made exactly at the point directed.
texts.marginal: SP met the 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL minima before every turn after takeoff, but each turn was begun within a few knots and a few tens of feet of those minima. The gates were never violated and no prompting was required. SP is expected to let the acceleration and the climb develop further before the first turn, so that both minima are met with margin.

texts_at.0: SP climbed straight ahead after takeoff with the IP calling out 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL as each gate was reached, due to first exposure to holding the climb straight ahead until both gates are confirmed rather than turning at a point on the ground. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to confirm 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL and begin the turn independently on the next departure, without the gates being called.
texts_at.1: SP climbed straight ahead and began the first turn after takeoff to the level expected at this stage, with 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL only just reached before the roll began, due to the turn point being anticipated from the routing rather than confirmed from the two gates themselves. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm both 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL from the instruments before starting the turn, not from the anticipated routing.
texts_at.2: SP rolled wings level and continued straight ahead until both 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL were attained, correcting without prompting, due to a scan concentrated on the turn point rather than on airspeed and altitude that let the bank begin a moment before the gates were confirmed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the scan on airspeed and altitude until both gates are confirmed before shifting it to the turn point.
texts_at.3: SP climbed straight ahead past the departure end of the runway and attained a minimum of 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL before the first turn, due to the confirmation of both gates coming a couple of seconds after they were actually reached rather than the instant they were met. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm each gate the instant it is reached rather than a few seconds later.

texts_above.1: SP climbed straight ahead and began the first turn after takeoff with 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL only just reached before the roll began. The gates were confirmed after a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP started to bank before 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL had been confirmed, then recognized the anticipation, rolled wings level and continued straight ahead until both values were attained, correcting without prompting and losing only a short segment of the departure track. Holding the scan on airspeed and altitude until both gates are confirmed, rather than shifting it to the turn point early, would remove the anticipation from the departure. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good gate discipline after takeoff.
texts_above.3: SP climbed straight ahead until past the departure end of the runway and attained a minimum of 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL before the first turn after takeoff, with the turn flown onto the published departure track and heading held within 5 degrees. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good gate discipline after takeoff.
texts_above.4: SP confirmed the departure end, 140 KIAS and 700 feet AGL as distinct gates and rolled into the first turn at the exact point required, with heading and track deviations negligible and the climb rate preserved through the turn. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent gate discipline after takeoff.

error_modes.label: Wake turbulence anticipation and selection of the takeoff point

texts.0: SP, due to failing to anticipate wake turbulence when taking off behind another aircraft on the same runway with the wind straight down the runway, did not plan the takeoff point. The takeoff was made past the preceding aircraft's takeoff point and before their point of touchdown, and the aircraft rolled uncommanded in the initial climb with deviations beyond anything the criteria allow. IP took the controls to recover wings level and clear the wake.
texts.1: SP, due to not accounting for the preceding aircraft's takeoff point with the wind calm, planned a takeoff point that left no margin against wake turbulence. The initial climb was flown through disturbed air with attitude and alignment deviations at the limit of the allowed values, and the flight path was moved away from the wake only after IP prompted for it.
texts.2: SP, due to identifying the preceding aircraft late in the pattern, initially set up for a takeoff point close to the wake of that aircraft. SP re-evaluated the wind and the preceding takeoff point on personal initiative and adjusted the plan before brake release, so the exposure produced only intermediate deviations, corrected in time and without prompting.
texts.3: SP anticipated wake turbulence behind the preceding aircraft on the same runway and planned to take off at a point prior to that aircraft's takeoff point. The initial climb stayed clear of the wake and the departure was flown within the code 3 tolerances.
texts.4: SP identified the wake turbulence threat before line up, stated the wind and the preceding aircraft's takeoff point, and selected a takeoff point that kept the flight path clear of the wake. The departure was flown with negligible deviations and no wake encounter.
texts.marginal: SP anticipated the wake turbulence and chose an acceptable takeoff point, but the plan relied on the preceding aircraft rotating where it usually does rather than on what was observed. The takeoff was flown clear of the wake and within standards. SP is expected to base the takeoff point on the observed rotation point of the preceding aircraft and on the actual wind.

texts_at.0: SP planned the takeoff point relative to the preceding aircraft with the IP calling attention to that aircraft's takeoff point and the wind, due to first exposure to weighing wake turbulence against another aircraft's position on the same runway. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to identify the preceding aircraft's takeoff point and plan around it independently on the next departure, without it being pointed out.
texts_at.1: SP planned the takeoff point relative to the preceding aircraft to the level expected at this stage, with the initial climb kept clear of the worst of the wake, due to the preceding aircraft's takeoff point being identified only after the wind was already assessed rather than in the same look. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to identify the preceding aircraft's takeoff point and the wind together, as one combined assessment.
texts_at.2: SP re-evaluated the wind and the preceding aircraft's takeoff point on personal initiative and adjusted the plan before brake release, due to the preceding aircraft being identified late in the pattern that initially set up a takeoff point close to its wake. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to identify the preceding aircraft's position earlier in the pattern so the takeoff point is set without needing a late adjustment.
texts_at.3: SP anticipated wake turbulence behind the preceding aircraft and planned a takeoff point prior to that aircraft's own takeoff point, due to the final adjustment for wind being made a few seconds later than the takeoff-point selection rather than as part of the same assessment. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to fold the wind check into the same assessment as the takeoff-point selection.

texts_above.1: SP planned a takeoff point relative to the preceding aircraft, with the initial climb flown through some disturbed air before the flight path was adjusted clear of the wake. The adjustment followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP identified the preceding aircraft late in the pattern and initially set up for a takeoff point close to its wake, then re-evaluated the wind and the preceding takeoff point on personal initiative and adjusted the plan before brake release, so the exposure produced only intermediate deviations, corrected in time. Identifying the preceding aircraft's position earlier in the pattern, rather than adjusting late, would remove the need for that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound wake-turbulence planning.
texts_above.3: SP anticipated wake turbulence behind the preceding aircraft on the same runway and planned to take off at a point prior to that aircraft's takeoff point, with the initial climb staying clear of the wake and the departure flown within the code 3 tolerances. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed wake-turbulence planning.
texts_above.4: SP identified the wake turbulence threat before line up, stated the wind and the preceding aircraft's takeoff point, and selected a takeoff point that kept the flight path clear of the wake, with the departure flown with negligible deviations and no wake encounter. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional wake-turbulence planning.
